summary.text: Jim Risch is the incumbent Republican U.S. Senator from Idaho, first elected in 2008 and now serving his third term. A lawyer and rancher by background, he spent decades in Idaho politics as a county prosecutor, state senator, lieutenant governor and, briefly, governor before joining the Senate. According to his Senate website, he chairs the Foreign Relations Committee and also serves on the Energy and Natural Resources, Small Business and Entrepreneurship, Intelligence and Ethics committees.

paragraphs.text: Risch was born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, and attended the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee from 1961 to 1963 before moving to the University of Idaho.
He received a bachelor's degree in forestry in 1965 and a law degree in 1968 from the University of Idaho, where he served on the Law Review.

He was elected Ada County Prosecuting Attorney in 1970 and served two terms, and during that time he taught criminal justice classes at Boise State University and served as president of the Idaho Prosecuting Attorneys Association.

Risch served in the Idaho State Senate from 1975 to 1988 and again from 1995 to 2002; his Senate website says his Republican colleagues elected him Majority Leader and President Pro Tempore. According to Wikipedia, he lost a 1988 re-election bid and returned to the chamber in 1995 by appointment.

He then served as Idaho's lieutenant governor from 2003 to 2006, after which he became the state's 31st governor on May 26, 2006, when Gov. Dirk Kempthorne resigned to become U.S. Secretary of the Interior.
According to his Senate website, his governorship included property-tax reform that cut property taxes by 20% and $100 million in additional funding for public schools.
He returned to the lieutenant governor's office from 2007 to 2009.
Risch won the U.S. Senate seat on November 4, 2008, defeating Democrat Larry LaRocco, 57.7% to 34.1%, and took office in 2009.
He was re-elected in 2014, defeating Democrat Nels Mitchell, 65.3% to 34.7%, and in 2020, defeating Democrat Paulette Jordan, 62.6% to 33.2%.

Outside public service, he is a rancher, small business owner and former senior partner in the Risch Goss Insinger Gustavel law firm; he and his wife, Vicki, have been married for more than 50 years, have three sons and nine grandchildren, and live on a ranch outside Boise, according to his Senate website.
